idiom_name: struct of acquire/release function pointers (or macro-selected policy) over POSIX or C11 primitives
implementation_notes: C has no polymorphism and no destructors, so the locking strategy is a hand-written vtable: a lock object plus pointers to acquire/release functions, or a macro that selects the policy at compile time. The strategy family comes from the platform - POSIX mutexes whose type is fixed at initialization with pthread_mutexattr_settype (PTHREAD_MUTEX_NORMAL, PTHREAD_MUTEX_ERRORCHECK, PTHREAD_MUTEX_RECURSIVE, PTHREAD_MUTEX_DEFAULT), pthread_rwlock_t for reader/writer policies, semaphores, or C11 <threads.h> mtx_t created with mtx_plain, mtx_recursive or mtx_timed. Because there is no scope-based reclamation, the Scoped Locking half of the design must be emulated with a single-exit structure or a goto-cleanup block that releases on every path; when a component is used with exactly one policy forever, calling pthread_mutex_lock/unlock directly is simpler.
pitfalls: Without RAII every return path must release the lock; an early return added later silently deadlocks the component, so enforce a single-exit or goto-cleanup convention.
The indirect call through the ops struct defeats inlining, so a no-op policy still costs a call per critical section unless the policy is fixed with macros and compiled away.

The POSIX mutex type is fixed at initialization and <threads.h> is not available everywhere, so a policy swap that forgets pthread_mutexattr_settype silently yields a non-recursive or error-checking mutex.
